ann_82.text: Across the whole model, a higher daytime charge (19.07 to 42.40 US dollars) clearly raises the predicted chance of leaving, and this part makes it even more so for customers with 180 daytime minutes or fewer: from about 2% to about 47%, against below 1% to about 19% above that.

Through this part itself, the daytime charge lowers it only while it stays below about 25.73 US dollars: for the typical customer, going from 15.49 to 59.76 US dollars moves it from about 11% to about 3%, and across the usual range it slightly lowers it (on the training data only).
For the typical customer this part acts on (one with 2 customer-service calls and about 131 daytime minutes), customer-service calls (0 to 3) slightly raise it from about 3% to about 6%.
This part acts on 1341 of 4000 customers, 200 of whom left; for the typical one it slightly raises the chance from about 2% to about 3%.
In Nebraska the daytime charge counts slightly more: from below 1% to about 27% there, against about 1% to about 23% elsewhere.
For a typical customer in Alabama, calls slightly add to it from 4 calls upwards, from about 3% to about 6% (the model has little data on this: 16 customers there are past that point).

ann_83.text: Through this part, more daytime minutes clearly lower the predicted chance of leaving only while they stay below about 194 minutes: for the typical customer, going from 91 to 352 minutes moves it from about 24% to about 2%.
Customer-service calls clearly add to it from 2 calls upwards: for a typical such customer, going from 0 to 4 calls moves it from about 3% to about 9%.
Across the usual range, more daytime minutes (112 to 249) clearly lower it from about 15% to about 2% through this part.
Daytime minutes slightly lower it more when the evening charge is 17.12 US dollars or less: from about 17% to about 1%, against about 15% to about 3%.
This part acts on 2378 of 4000 customers, 249 of whom left; for the typical one (with about 153 daytime minutes) it slightly raises the chance from about 1% to about 2%.
A higher evening charge slightly lowers it from about 6% to about 2% (on the training data only).

ann_84.text: Through this part, a higher night-time charge slightly adds to the predicted chance of leaving once it rises above about 8.79 US dollars, and more daytime minutes slightly lower it once they rise above about 124 minutes, both staying at about 2% to 3% for the typical customer (on the training data only).

ann_85.text: Through this part, being in Nevada, Maryland, New Jersey or Maine slightly raises the predicted chance of leaving to about 3%, and Missouri slightly lowers it to about 2% (on the training data only).

ann_86.text: Through this part, a higher daytime charge clearly raises the typical customer's predicted chance of leaving from below 1% to about 23%, and an international plan clearly raises it from about 3% to about 20%.
California and Washington raise it to about 10% compared with West Virginia (on the training data only).
A higher evening charge slightly raises it from about 1% to about 5%, and a voice-mail plan slightly lowers it to about 1%.

Michigan slightly raises it to about 7%, Montana to about 6%, Tennessee, Kentucky, Utah, Ohio and Maine to about 4% and several other states to about 3%, while Hawaii slightly lowers it to below 1% and Vermont, Colorado, Rhode Island, Alaska, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Alabama, Georgia and New Hampshire to about 1% to 2% (on the training data only).

More international and evening minutes, more voice-mail messages, a longer account, more daytime calls and a higher night-time charge slightly raise it, while more international, evening and night-time calls and area codes 408 and 510 slightly lower it (on the training data only).

ann_82.original: HYPOTHESIS: 776 = relu(-0.567 + 1.565*relu(0.603*CSC-0.325) - 0.086*relu(0.993*CSC-0.196) - 0.782*day - 0.138*state22 - 0.589*state29) (day = dayCharge = dayMinutes after z-scoring; -0.836*dayCharge + 0.054*dayMinutes), read out with +1.646 on the logit. It is a customer-service-calls x low-day-usage interaction. The CSC term turns on from 3 calls (6258) and grows linearly; the unit is on when day usage is below a threshold that rises with CSC: day z < -0.6 for 0-2 calls (a weak low-usage hinge), < 0.0 at 3 calls, < 0.8 at 4, < 1.6 at 5+. EVIDENCE (train, n=4000): on for 26% of rows with 0-2 calls but 78-100% with 4+ calls; mean logit contribution 0.2 (0-2 calls) -> 1.07 (4 calls) -> 3.6 (6 calls); among 4+ callers with low day usage (z<-0.5) churn is 0.87-1.0 and the unit adds +2.5 to +4.9. Linear fit R2 0.54; linearising it alone drops train AUC 0.905 -> 0.894; restoring it alone onto the fully linearised model gains +0.050 AUC. Sensitivity: dayCharge 0.28, state29 0.20, CSC 0.11. state29 (72 rows) switches the unit off entirely (z=7.4 gives -4.35 pre-activation): for the 28 state-29 rows where it would be on, it removes 0.95 logit on average (1 churner among them). state22 removes up to 0.86. These are rare-category switches. For 0-2 callers with very low day usage (z<-2, 93 rows) the unit and 4496 overshoot the direct day slope, giving a logit 0.7 above the empirical log-odds (mild U-shape artefact).
ann_82.proposed: Service calls with low daytime charge: the part lowers the chance of leaving as the daytime charge rises below about 25.73 US dollars, slightly raises it with calls, and makes the overall daytime-charge effect stronger for customers with 180 daytime minutes or fewer.

ann_83.original: HYPOTHESIS: 4496 = relu(-1.966 - 1.843*dayMinutes - 0.859*eveCharge + g(CSC)), read out with +0.809. g is a monotone piecewise-linear function of CSC from the chain 7068 = relu(0.577*CSC-0.148) (on from 2 calls) -> 7561, 11555, 12924, 9009 (always on, so affine in 7068) plus 10362 = relu(0.933*7068-0.505) (on from 4 calls, an extra kink); g = 2.23 at 0-1 calls, 2.30 at 2, then about +0.8 per extra call (3.04 at 3, 3.88 at 4, 5.58 at 6). So 4496 is a below-average day+evening usage hinge (0.26 - 1.84*day - 0.86*eve > 0 at 0-1 calls) whose threshold and height rise with service calls. EVIDENCE (train): on for 52% of 0-call rows, 82% at 4 calls, 100% at 7+; mean logit contribution 0.74 at 0 calls, 1.56 at 4, 3.65 at 6. With the +1.92 direct dayCharge edge it makes the day effect convex: slope 1.92 above average usage, 0.43 below (and about -0.86 below z=-0.73 together with 776). Linear fit R2 0.78; linearising it alone drops train AUC 0.905 -> 0.889; restoring it alone onto the fully linearised model gains +0.056. Sensitivity: dayMinutes 1.09, eveCharge 0.51, CSC 0.29. eveCharge equals eveMinutes after z-scoring (the backbone also uses both).
ann_83.proposed: Low usage with service calls: fewer daytime minutes raise the chance of leaving below about 194 minutes (about 24% to 2% from 91 to 352 minutes), and customer-service calls add to it from 2 calls upwards.

ann_84.original: HYPOTHESIS: two small single-input hinges, 10224 = relu(1.057 + 1.004*dayMinutes) (weight -0.067; on for 86% of rows, off below day z=-1.05) and 15615 = relu(0.102 + 1.007*nightCharge) (weight +0.108; on above night z=-0.10). They slightly bend the linear day and night slopes. EVIDENCE (train): logit sd 0.09, linear R2 0.84, linearising them changes train AUC by <0.001 (0.9052 -> 0.9050); restoring them alone onto the linearised model gains nothing (-0.001). Functionally negligible. nightCharge equals nightMinutes after z-scoring (nightMinutes is unconnected).
ann_84.proposed: Two small bends on the night-time charge and daytime minutes; all slight and on the training data only.

ann_85.original: HYPOTHESIS: four relu units over state one-hots that are always on (biases 0.34-1.37 exceed the inactive z of about -0.15), so they are exact affine state offsets: 4171 = relu(1.369 + 0.072*state24 - 0.048*state33) read out -0.837 (state24 -0.42 logit, state33 +0.29), 9698 state31 +0.19, 13306 state20 +0.21, 16618 state21 +0.18 (plus 0.09 direct). EVIDENCE (train): every unit active on 100% of the 4000 rows, linear R2 1.0, linearising changes nothing. Pure one-hot offsets on 77-90-row categories.
ann_85.proposed: Slight state offsets for Nevada, Maryland, New Jersey, Maine and Missouri, on the training data only.

ann_86.original: HYPOTHESIS: the identity node identity_lin sums the 42 direct input->output edges, an additive logit backbone. Per z unit: dayCharge +1.92 (the dominant term; it also equals dayMinutes), internationalPlan +0.67, voiceMailPlan -0.69 with numberVmailMessages +0.14, eveCharge +0.60 and eveMinutes +0.15 (identical after z-scoring, net +0.74), intlMinutes +0.18, intlCalls -0.17, accountLength +0.13, dayCalls +0.12, nightCharge +0.11, and 31 small state/area-code offsets. Because a state z is ~7 when active, state coefficients of -0.35 (state11), -0.25 (state46), +0.15 (state47), +0.12 (state4), -0.15 (state39, state5), -0.10 (state0, state38) give offsets of 0.7-2.6 logit on 41-82-row categories, closely matching the in-sample calibrating offset for each state. Exactly linear by construction (closed-form error 0.007 from coefficient rounding).
ann_86.proposed: A linear backbone in which the daytime charge (below 1% to about 23%) and an international plan (about 3% to 20%) raise the chance of leaving and a voice-mail plan slightly lowers it; California and Washington raise it to about 10% on the training data only.

ann_87.original: HYPOTHESIS: logit P(churn) = -2.70 + linear_backbone + 1.646*csc_lowday_gate + 0.809*csc_lowusage_hinge - 0.067*h_day + 0.108*h_night + state offsets (-0.837*4171 + 0.029*9698 + 0.031*13306 + 0.027*16618): a purely additive combination of the children at the output sigmoid. The 24 unconnected inputs (21 states, areaCode415, nightMinutes, intlCharge) have zero effect. EVIDENCE (train): full AUC 0.905; refit L2 LR 0.843; all non-backbone children replaced by their least-squares linear fits 0.839. The gain over linear (+0.066) comes almost entirely from the two CSC x usage units: restoring either alone recovers +0.050 (776) or +0.056 (4496), together 0.905; the usage hinges and state units add nothing. They encode the known churn pattern that heavy service callers (4+ calls) churn unless their day usage is high (churn 0.87-1.0 at low day usage vs 0.14 at day z 0.5-1), together with the convex high-day-usage effect. State effects are one-hot offsets plus a state29 switch that disables 776.
ann_87.proposed: The model adds a linear backbone, two customer-service parts tied to low daytime usage, small usage hinges and state offsets; a higher daytime charge (about 1% to 23%) and an international plan (about 3% to 20%) raise the chance of leaving, more daytime minutes lower it (about 16% to 2%), and the international charge and night-time minutes are ignored.

summary.text: For a typical customer (one in West Virginia with area code 415, an account length of 100, no international or voice-mail plan, one customer-service call and median usage such as 180 daytime minutes), the model predicts about a 3% chance that the customer leaves, and an international plan clearly raises that to about 20%.
A higher daytime charge (19.07 to 42.40 US dollars) clearly raises it from about 1% to about 23%, while more daytime minutes (112 to 249) clearly lower it from about 16% to about 2%.
Through one part, more daytime minutes clearly lower it only while they stay below about 194 minutes: for the typical customer, going from 91 to 352 minutes moves it from about 24% to about 2%.
Through the same part, customer-service calls clearly add to it from 2 calls upwards: for a typical such customer, going from 0 to 4 calls moves it from about 3% to about 9%.
Being in California or Washington rather than West Virginia raises it to about 10% (on the training data only).

Across the usual range, customer-service calls (0 to 3) slightly raise it to about 5% and a voice-mail plan slightly lowers it to about 1%, and the model ignores the international charge and night-time minutes.

It is a customer-service-calls x low-day-usage interaction. The CSC term turns on from 3 calls (6258) and grows linearly; the unit is on when day usage is below a threshold that rises with CSC: day z < -0.6 for 0-2 calls (a weak low-usage hinge), < 0.0 at 3 calls, < 0.8 at 4, < 1.6 at 5+.
